abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Relapse after chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T‐cell therapy in large B‐cell lymphoma (LBCL) is associated with a dismal prognosis. Although Phase 3 trials have established CAR T‐cells as standard second‐line (2L) therapy, outcomes and optimal management after relapse in this setting remain unknown because no real‐world data are currently available. We conducted a multicenter retrospective study using the French DESCAR‐T registry, including patients with LBCL who relapsed after 2L CAR T‐cell therapy with axicabtagene ciloleucel or lisocabtagene maraleucel. The objective was to describe postrelapse treatments, outcomes, and prognostic factors. Among the 893 patients treated with 2L CAR T‐cells, 297 (33%) relapsed and were analyzed. Median time to relapse was 2.7 months, with 35% of these relapses occurring within 2 months. Among the 231 treated patients, bispecific antibody (BsAb)‐based regimens were the most common type of salvage therapy (65%). The overall response rate after relapse was 39.1%, with a complete response rate of 27.6%. Notably, despite the use of BsAb‐based therapy in 65% of patients, the median overall survival (OS2) after relapse was only 6.5 months (median progression‐free survival [PFS2]: 3.4 months). Patients treated with BsAb monotherapy achieved a median OS of 7.1 months. Multivariate analysis revealed that early relapse (<6 months), an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) ≥ 2, and an elevated C‐reactive protein (≥30 mg/L) were independently associated with poor OS. This study represents the first real‐world analysis of outcomes after relapse following 2L CAR T‐cell therapy. Despite the more frequent incorporation of BsAbs into the therapeutic landscape, overall prognosis and treatment efficacy remain dismal, highlighting the urgent need for innovative therapeutic strategies and dedicated prospective trials in this emerging double‐refractory population.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Anti‐CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T‐cells have shown impressive results in the treatment of relapsed/refractory (R/R) aggressive large B‐cell lymphoma (LBCL) as a third‐ or higher‐line (3L+) therapy, leading to the first approval of this treatment for patients with LBCL. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 Registry‐based studies with patients who relapsed after 3L+ CAR T‐cell therapy from DESCAR‐T and collaborative cohorts in the United Kingdom/Spain have consistently shown median overall survival (OS) of approximately 5–6 months, with even shorter survival among patients who relapse within the first 30–60 days after infusion. 5 , 6 , 7 Although novel strategies such as bispecific antibodies (BsAbs) or targeted therapy regimens may induce responses, durable disease control is uncommon. 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 Therefore, relapse after 3L+ CAR T‐cell therapy in LBCL is associated with poor prognosis, with no established salvage standard and only limited evidence to guide management. 11 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17

More recently, Phase 3 trials (ZUMA‐7, TRANSFORM) have established CAR T‐cell therapy as the new standard‐of‐care (SOC) in second‐line (2L) therapy for transplant‐eligible patients with early relapsed or refractory LBCL, and these trials have demonstrated superior survival compared with conventional salvage chemotherapy. 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 Phase 2 studies (PILOT, ALYCANTE) further extended this approach to older or high‐risk, transplant‐ineligible patients, confirming the feasibility and efficacy of axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi‐cel) and lisocabtagene maraleucel (liso‐cel) in 2L settings. 22 , 23 All of this data led to the approval of this treatment as a 2L therapy for patients with LBCL in 2022. For LBCL patients with refractory disease or early relapse (<12 months) who are deemed eligible for CAR T‐cells, axi‐cel and liso‐cel now represent the SOC in 2L therapy in published international guidelines. 16 , 17 , 24

Patients who receive 2L CAR T‐cell therapy, either axi‐cel or liso‐cel, usually present with high‐risk clinical features, including primary refractory disease or early relapse (R/R12) following first‐line chemoimmunotherapy. 18 , 20 , 22 , 23 , 25 In contrast, virtually no real‐world prospective data exist to guide the management of patients who relapse after 2L CAR T‐cell therapy. Apart from exploratory postprotocol analyses of the ZUMA‐7 Phase 3 study, the literature is remarkably scarce for this growing and particularly refractory patient population across treatment groups. 19 , 26

In this context, systematic evaluation of treatment patterns and outcomes after relapse following 2L CAR T‐cell therapy is critical. Defining prognosis and therapeutic efficacy in this setting will guide clinical decision‐making and support the design of future strategies for LBCL patients who remain in urgent need of effective salvage options. In this context, we performed a large multicenter analysis of data from the French DESCAR‐T registry to describe treatment patterns, outcomes, and prognostic factors in patients with LBCL relapsing after 2L CAR T‐cell therapy.

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p: Patients with relapsed or refractory LBCL who experienced disease progression after 2L CAR T‐cell therapy with axi‐cel or liso‐cel were included in the present analysis from the DESCAR‐T registry. Data from 34 participating centers were collected between August 2022 and September 2024 and analyzed as of September 1, 2024. Patients' nonopposition to participation in this study was obtained through a written information note provided before inclusion in the registry. DESCAR‐T is registered under the ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT04328298, 27 and the study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary endpoint was overall survival after post‐CAR T‐cell relapse (OS2). Secondary endpoints included overall response rate (ORR2), complete response rate (CRR2), progression‐free survival (PFS2), duration of response (DOR2), and PFS2/OS2 according to the type of salvage treatment. PFS2 was measured from the start of salvage therapy to disease progression, relapse, death from any cause, or last follow‐up, whichever occurred first. OS2 was calculated from the start of salvage therapy to death from any cause or last follow‐up. Responses were assessed by local investigators per Lugano 2014 criteria using 18F‐FDG PET imaging, 28 , 29 and the best overall response was considered. DOR2 was defined as the time from the first documented response (complete response [CR] or partial response [PR]) to disease progression, relapse, death, or last follow‐up.

sec.title: Subgroups analyses
sec.p: Salvage treatments administered after CAR T‐cell therapy failure were categorized into four groups: BsAbs in monotherapy (BI); BsAb‐based combinations (BIC, BsAbs combined with chemotherapy, or immunomodulatory drugs [IMiDs]); chemotherapy or chemoimmunotherapy (CH, such as DHA[OX/C/P] or ICE regimens); and other therapies, including targeted agents, IMiDs, or radiotherapy.

Based on previously reported prognostic factors for relapse after 3L+ CAR T‐cell therapy, subgroup analyses were conducted to identify or validate predictors of outcome in patients relapsing after 2L CAR T‐cell therapy. 6 , 11 , 30 , 31 We hypothesized that patients receiving CH or “other” therapies would exhibit distinct clinicobiological characteristics compared with those treated with BsAbs, while potential differences between BI and BIC were assessed separately. To minimize confounding bias, propensity‐score–based matching was performed between the different treatment groups.

Time from CAR T‐cell infusion to relapse was analyzed as a continuous variable in months, as this approach proved most informative and discriminative for both PFS and OS; predefined cutoffs (e.g., 3 months) were not applied, although the 6‐month threshold has been reported as clinically relevant in the literature. 6 , 32

sec.title: Matching procedures
sec.p: Methodological innovation (four treatment groups instead of two to balance) required a new algorithm compared to binary groups previously described in the DESCAR‐T group. 33 Propensity scores and subsequent weights were estimated via a gradient boosted multivariate logistic regression model (GBW) with the type of treatment group as the dependent variable. GBW results in a pseudo‐population balanced with respect to the distribution of patient covariates in each group. The methodology underlying propensity‐score–based comparisons has been reviewed elsewhere. 34 An exhaustive list of covariates, described and presented in Table S1, was used for GBW. For all weighting parameters except continuous variables (no missing values were allowed for continuous covariates in GBW), missing data were considered as the worst‐case category. In the case of missing data for one parameter, the value was always less than 10%. The overall balance of GBW was assessed using the maximum of the pairwise absolute mean differences between all two‐by‐two group comparisons.
Conversely, subgroup analyses assessing the impact of time to relapse and the comparison between specific BsAbs were performed in the unweighted population.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Survival distributions were compared through the log‐rank test. Response rates were compared via the χ 2 test. A two‐sided P value of less than 0.05 was considered significant. No adjustment was performed for multiple testing. Survival curves were generated by using the Kaplan–Meier estimation method. Cutoff for time between infusion and treatment for progression was calculated using previously described methods. 35 Univariate Cox regression was used to assess the prognostic value of clinicobiological parameters at relapse after CAR T‐cell infusion for PFS and OS. For multivariate analysis (MVA), clinicobiological variables were included, using Cox models, which were significant in univariate analysis (UVA; with P ≤ 0.25) and remained in the model after backward selection on Akaike Information Criterion. Statistical analyses were performed with SAS software version 9.4.

sec.title: Demographic and baseline characteristics
sec.p: Among the 893 patients with R/R LBCL treated with 2L CAR T‐cell therapy in the DESCAR‐T registry from August 2022 until September 2024, 297 patients (33%) experienced disease progression and were included in the patient population for this analysis.

At the time of CAR T‐cell indication or before lymphodepletion, most patients had diffuse large B‐cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (DLBCL‐NOS; n = 217, 73.1%), with high‐risk clinical features. Most presented with an age‐adjusted IPI score of 2–3 (n = 158, 66.4%), disease refractory to first‐line chemoimmunotherapy (n = 222, 77.4%), and elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels (n = 165, 55.7%). High tumor burden was common, with bulky disease in 23.8% (n = 67) of patients, and central nervous system involvement was observed in 7% (n = 12) of patients. sec.p: At the time of infusion, patients received either axi‐cel (n = 253, 85%) or liso‐cel (n = 44, 15%). Among the 297 patients who subsequently relapsed after 2L CAR T‐cell therapy, the best response following CAR T‐cell infusion was initial complete or partial remission in 64.3% (n = 191; CR 34.7%, PR 29.6%), whereas 35.7% (n = 106) had stable or progressive disease. A comparison of baseline clinical and biological features among the 297 patients who ultimately progressed revealed no significant differences between those achieving an initial response (CR/PR) and those with stable or progressive disease (SD/PD) after CAR T‐cells (Table S2).

With a median follow‐up since CAR T‐cell infusion of 12.1 months (interquartile range [IQR], 11.3–12.3), the median time from CAR T‐cell infusion to relapse was 2.7 months (IQR, 1.2–3.3). Overall, 35% of patients (n = 104) relapsed within 2 months, 53% (n = 158) between 2 and 6 months, and 12% (n = 35) beyond 6 months. With a 3‐month cutoff, 43.2% (n = 105) of patients experienced early relapse after CAR T‐cell therapy.

At first relapse, the median patient age was 61.2 years (range, 25–82), with 24% aged ≥70 years (n = 71) and 47.1% presenting an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status ≥2 (n = 132). Elevated LDH levels (>upper limit of normal [ULN]) were detected in 48.4% (n = 89) of the patients, and C‐reactive protein [CRP] ≥ 30 mg/L was detected in 7.8% (n = 14) of the patients. Detailed characteristics at relapse are provided in Table 1.

sec.title: Treatment at the time of failure
sec.p: Among the 297 patients who relapsed after 2L CAR T‐cell therapy, 231 (78%) initiated salvage treatment within a median of 15 days following documentation of relapse (IQR, 7–34). The 66 patients excluded from the analysis represented a heterogeneous group that included untreated cases, patients who deceased before treatment initiation, and patients with insufficient follow‐up or missing data; therefore, these patients were not suitable for direct comparison of salvage strategies. Among the 231 treated patients, BsAb‐based regimens were the most frequent (65%), including 121 patients (52.4%) who received monotherapy (BI) and 29 (12.6%) who received combination therapy (BIC). Chemotherapy or chemoimmunotherapy and other treatments accounted for 12.6% (n = 29) and 22.5% (n = 52) of the cases, respectively (Table 2). Within the chemotherapy or chemoimmunotherapy group, no patients received allogeneic stem cell transplantation, and only three patients underwent autologous stem cell transplantation. Apart from earlier relapse observed among patients who received BIC compared with those who received BI (P = 0.008), no significant differences in baseline clinical or biological features were detected between these two BsAb subgroups (Table S3).

sec.title: Propensity score matching
sec.p: In the present study, the aim of PSM was to balance covariates between the treatment groups at relapse after CAR T‐cell failure to account for all possible measured confounding variables. These variables have already been shown in the literature to affect PFS and OS after R/R CAR T‐cell therapy and are potential confounders bias. 5 , 6 , 26 , 32 , 36 After propensity score weighting, covariate balance across treatment groups was satisfactory considering the expected inflation related to the increased number of groups to be balanced and the observational nature of the study, with absolute standardized mean differences (ASMDs) below 0.3 for all variables (Table S5). The matched population is detailed in Table S6. The key baseline characteristics, particularly the Ann Arbor stage, sex ratio, CRP, ECOG performance status, time from CAR T‐cell infusion to progression, and CAR T‐cell product type, were well balanced.

sec.title: Response efficacy
sec.p: Among 156 evaluable patients who received salvage regimens after CAR T‐cell failure, the ORR2 was 39.1% (n = 61), including a CR rate of 27.6% (n = 43) and a PR rate of 11.5% (n = 18).

The ORR rate after salvage treatment was 39.5% in the BI group, 29.4% in the BIC group, 50% in the CH group, and 33.3% in the other treatment group, with corresponding CR rates of 29.6%, 10.9%, 41.7%, and 18.1%, respectively (Figure 1).

sec.title: Outcomes after failure of CAR T therapy
sec.p: After a median follow‐up of 8.4 months since the initiation of salvage therapy (IQR, 3.4–11.3), the median PFS2 was 3.4 months (95% CI, 3.0–3.9). The 6‐month and estimated 1‐year PFS2 rates were 32.5% (26.3–38.9) and 25.0% (18.5–32.1), respectively (Figure 2A). In the weighted analysis, median PFS2 by treatment group was 3.7 months (2.7–4.7) for BI, 2.9 months (1.7–4.1) for BIC, 2.4 months (1.0–6.3) for CH, and 1.7 months (1.3–2.3) for other therapies (Figure 2B). PFS2 was numerically longer in the BI group than in the others group (hazard ratio [HR], 0.58; 0.37–0.89; P < 0.001). The median OS2 was 6.5 months (95% CI, 5.6–7.9). The 6‐month and estimated 1‐year OS2 rates were 53.7% (46.8–60.2) and 36.1% (28.7–43.5), respectively (Figure 3A). In the weighted analysis, median OS2 by treatment group was 7.1 months (5.4–NA) for BI, 4.9 months (3.2–9.2) for BIC, 6.3 months (2.4–14.4) for CH, and 5.9 months (2.3–9.0) for other therapies (Figure 3B). OS2 was numerically longer with BI than with the other regimens (HR 1.30 [CH vs. BI, 0.76–2.24]; 0.55 [BI vs. BIC, 0.31–0.95]; and 0.64 [BI vs. other, 0.40–1.03]; global P = 0.0094) (Figure 2A,B). The median DOR2 was not reached (NR, 95% CI, 5.8–NR). The 6‐month and 1‐year DOR2 rates were 65.6% (48.4–78.3) and 59.6% (40.0–74.7), respectively (Figure 4A). In the weighted analysis, median DOR2 by treatment group was NR for BI, 3.1 months (1.0–3.1) for BIC, 5.1 months (0.7–NR) for CH, and NR for other therapies (Figure 4B).

sec.title: Efficacy and outcomes in subgroup analysis
sec.p: Regarding the time from CAR T‐cell infusion to disease progression, CR rates were higher in patients with late relapse: 15.6% when ≤2 months (n = 12), 16.5% in the range of 2–6 months (n = 21), and 37% (n = 10) when >6 months, respectively. The median PFS2 and OS2 were significantly better in patients with late relapse (>6 months after CAR T‐cell infusion), with 8.1 months for late relapse >6 months (95% CI, 4.5‐NA, P < 0.001) and 13.4 months (95% CI, NA‐NA), respectively (Figure 5A,B, P = 0.011).

sec.p: In the subgroup analysis of BsAbs, no significant differences in PFS2 or OS2 were observed between glofitamab and epcoritamab—median PFS2/OS2 for glofitamab of 4 months (95% CI, 2.7–NA)/9.5 months (95% CI, 6.2–NA) and median PFS2/OS2 for epcoritamab, 2 months (95% CI, 1.3–8.6)/5.3 months (95% CI, 2.1–NA), HR: 1.55 (95% CI, 0.857–2.798) and HR: 1.48 (95% CI, 0.758–2.905) (Figure S1).

sec.title: Prognostic factors
sec.p: According to UVA, the following variables assessed at relapse were associated with longer PFS2: ECOG performance status 0–1 versus ≥2 (HR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.49–0.97; P = 0.021), longer time from infusion to progression (per 1‐month increase; HR, 0.81; 0.73–0.90; P < 0.001), and a better response to CAR T‐cell therapy (CR/PR vs. SD/PD; HR, 0.50; 0.36–0.71; P < 0.001). No significant associations were observed for other variables (Table S7). According to MVA, only the time between CAR T‐cell infusion and first progression (per 1‐month increase, HR, 0.822; 95% CI, 0.713–0.948; P = 0.0069) remained an independent predictor of PFS2 at relapse after 2L CAR T‐cell therapy (Table 3).

sec.p: With respect to factors associated with progression and OS2, UVA revealed several variables linked to longer survival: an ECOG performance status of 0–1 versus ≥2 (HR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.44–0.93; P = 0.02), CRP < 30 mg/L (HR, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.17–0.87; P = 0.021), a higher hemoglobin level (per 1 g/dL; HR, 0.91; 95% CI, 0.83–0.99; P = 0.046), a longer time from infusion to progression (per 1‐month increase; HR, 0.82; 95% CI, 0.72–0.93; P = 0.002), and a better response to CAR T‐cell therapy (CR/PR vs. SD/PD; HR, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.35–0.75; P < 0.001).

No significant associations were found for other factors, such as refractoriness to frontline therapy, histologic subtype, CAR T‐cell product, response to bridging therapy, LDH level, aaIPI score, Ann Arbor stage, bulky disease, or platelet and neutrophil counts at progression (Table S8).

After adjusting for these potential confounding factors in the MVA model, CRP < 30 mg/L (HR, 0.40; 95% CI, 0.17–0.92; P = 0.03), ECOG < 2 (HR, 0.58; 95% CI, 0.34–0.97; P = 0.038) and time between infusion and first progression (per 1 month, HR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.64–0.94; P = 0.011) remained independent OS2 predictors at the time of relapse after 2L CAR T‐cell therapy (Table 3).

Owing to the intrinsic collinearity between the HEMATOTOX score and variables significant in UVA (CRP and hemoglobin), separate analyses were performed to assess its prognostic impact. No significant differences were observed between the low‐ and high‐risk groups for either OS (0–1 vs. ≥2; HR, 1.25; 95% CI, 0.61–2.57; P = 0.54) or PFS (HR, 0.98; 95% CI, 0.53–1.79; P = 0.93) (data not shown).

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: This study provides the largest real‐world analysis of outcomes after relapse following 2L CAR T‐cell therapy in patients with LBCL. Among 893 patients treated with anti‐CD19 CAR T‐cells in the DESCAR‐T registry, one‐third (33%) experienced disease progression. A low ORR to salvage therapy (39.1%) was found, including a CR rate of 27.6%. Median PFS2 and OS2 were dramatically short, at 3.4 and 6.5 months, respectively. BsAb monotherapy resulted in slightly better outcomes than the other regimens did but remained particularly poor, with a median OS of 7.1 months, while early relapse within 6 months and elevated CRP levels were independently associated with inferior survival. Together, these findings highlight the dismal prognosis of this double‐refractory population—that failed both rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisolone (R‐CHOP) and CAR T‐cell therapy—and the very limited efficacy of current salvage approaches.

Comparable poor results were previously reported in a smaller cohort. Ghobadi et al. described poor outcomes in 59 patients who relapsed after 2L CAR T‐cell therapy in the ZUMA‐7 trial, with similarly short survival durations. 26 Among patients randomized to SOC, those receiving subsequent cellular immunotherapy achieved a median PFS of 6.3 months and an OS of 16.3 months, compared with 1.9 months and 9.5 months, respectively, for those receiving noncellular therapies. In contrast, patients who received 2L axi‐cel treatment and who required subsequent 3L therapy had markedly poorer outcomes: chemotherapy salvage resulted in a median PFS of 1.7 months and an OS of 8.1 months. Notably, the small subset (n = 8) of patients who received cellular immunotherapy (i.e., CAR T‐cell therapy) after axi‐cel achieved a median PFS of 3.5 months. Our findings extend these observations to a larger, unselected European cohort, providing critical real‐world evidence on treatment patterns and outcomes after the failure of 2L CAR T‐cell therapy.

Although 2L CAR T‐cell therapy appears to confer superior efficacy and survival compared with later‐line (L3+) administration, the prognosis of patients who relapse following 2L CAR T‐cell therapy remains as poor as that observed in patients who relapse after L3+ CAR T‐cell treatment. In the French DESCAR‐T analysis of 238 patients who progressed after receiving 3L CAR T‐cells therapy, outcomes were similarly poor, with median PFS and OS of 2.8 and 5.2 months, respectively. 5 A UK–Spanish collaborative study (n = 387) reported a median OS of 5.3 months after CAR T‐cell progression, with markedly shorter survival among patients relapsing within 2 months of infusion. 6 In comparison, the 6.5‐month median OS observed in our cohort after 2L CAR T‐cell failure represents only a nonimprovement, suggesting that disease biology—rather than treatment sequencing—is the predominant determinant of critical prognosis in this double‐refractory population, even though a greater proportion of patients in our cohort received more innovative and potentially more effective therapies (BsAbs for 65%) than those typically administered after L3+ CAR T‐cell relapse.

A critical finding from multiple prospective or retrospective analyses was that early relapse (≤6 months) after L3+ CAR T‐cell therapy predicted particularly poor efficacy and outcomes, including in patients who received subsequent BsAb therapy. 6 , 11 , 32 , 36 , 37 , 38 The current analysis extends these observations to the 2L CAR T‐cell real‐life setting, where 88% of patients relapsed within 6 months after CAR T‐cell infusion, with significantly worse PFS2 and OS2 than late relapse (>6 months), representing an enriched high‐risk population. Many contemporary trials in the post–CAR T setting exclude patients with early CAR T‐cell failure, particularly those relapsing within 3 months, despite representing the population with the greatest unmet clinical need. This is illustrated by several ongoing studies applying restrictive eligibility criteria or prolonged washout periods after CAR T‐cell therapy, including a CD19 × CD3 BsAb (NCT04594642), as well as emerging multitargeted or allogeneic strategies such as CD19/CD20/CD22 CAR T‐cells (NCT07168486), CD19/CD20 CAR T‐cells (NCT07335328), allogeneic CD19/CD20 CAR T‐cells (RN1701; NCT07316920), and the CD19‐directed degrader NX‐5948 (NCT05131022). This reinforces the biological aggressiveness of early‐relapsing disease and suggests that intrinsic resistance mechanisms persist across multiple immunotherapeutic approaches. Studies have demonstrated that early‐relapsing patients exhibit antigen escape, such as loss or downregulation of CD19 expression (20%–30% of relapsed patients) 39 , 40 or T‐cell dysfunction (poor CAR T‐cell expansion, reduced persistence, and T‐cell exhaustion phenotypes). 41 , 42 , 43 , 44 , 45 An effective early‐relapse detection strategy could combine close clinical monitoring, MRD/ctDNA assessment, CAR T‐cell tracking, and regular PET imaging until 6 months after CAR T‐cell infusion. This enables identification of relapse before clinical symptoms appear, allowing timely interventions such as BsAb therapy or enrollment in combinatorial immunotherapy clinical trials.

Beyond temporal patterns of relapse, the use of BsAbs has recently emerged as the most promising salvage option after 3L+ CAR T‐cell therapy, 11 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 but data concerning specific types of 2L CAR T‐cell failure have been lacking in both clinical trials and real‐world cohorts. The results of the present study, which included 150 patients who received a BsAb, provide a dataset supporting the relevance of the BsAbs after 2L CAR T‐cell therapy. In prior reports with BsAb after 3L+ CAR T‐cells, Shumilov et al. reported an ORR of 43% and a median OS of 7.7 months—reaching 10.5 months for late relapsers—whereas Iacoboni et al. reported ORR and CR rates of 51% and 36%, respectively, with 12‐month PFS and OS rates of 32% and 50%, respectively. 32 The prospective LYSA phase 2 BiCAR trial of glofitamab provides the first dedicated prospective evidence in this setting, with an ORR of 76%, a CR rate of 46%, a median PFS of 3.8 months, and a median OS of 14.7 months, with durable outcomes. 11 The ORR of 39.5% and CR rate of 29.6% observed in this study with BsAb monotherapy are lower than those previously reported in the 3L setting. This is further reflected by a median post‐CAR T‐cell survival of 7.1 months, which falls within the low range of the broader spectrum reported in earlier series after L3 CAR T‐cell failure. Moreover, although the BIC subgroup is inherently heterogeneous, this stratification was both statistically necessary to preserve balanced cohort sizes and clinically meaningful by providing an exploratory benchmark for emerging synergy‐based strategies currently being evaluated in major trials such as STARGLO (Glofitamab‐GemOx) and EPCORE (Epcoritamab‐combinations). These findings suggest that in these double‐refractory patients, BsAbs may overcome certain resistance mechanisms limiting CAR T‐cell efficacy, but they do not achieve outcomes comparable to those of patients receiving later lines of therapy, regardless of the type of BsAb used. The limited response to subsequent BsAb therapy among CAR T‐cell relapsers suggests the presence of cross‐resistance mechanisms affecting multiple T‐cell‐engaging immunotherapies. Alterations in the tumor microenvironment may contribute to this resistance through immunosuppressive features such as regulatory T‐cells, myeloid‐derived suppressor cells, and inhibitory cytokines that hinder both CAR T‐cell and BsAb activity. 46 , 47 , 48 , 49 , 50 , 51 In addition, intrinsic tumor factors—including high proliferative index, TP53 mutations, and complex karyotypes—are frequently enriched in relapsing patients and predict resistance to subsequent immunotherapies. 52 , 53 , 54 , 55 , 56 The optimal sequencing of 2L therapies remains a subject of intense debate. Although the STARGLO‐like approach (Glofitamab‐GemOx) has emerged as an option, its efficacy in patients refractory or relapsing <12 months after frontline therapy does not clearly surpass that of 2L CAR T‐cells (CR 59%, median OS 19 months, median PFS 9 months). 57 Furthermore, no data currently exist concerning the salvageability of patients for whom 2L BsAb‐based regimens fail. Our findings highlight that, while outcomes after 2L CAR T failure are modest (median OS of 6.5 months), shifting the sequence requires further prospective validation to ensure that 3L CAR T‐cell efficacy is not compromised by prior BsAb exposure in this double‐refractory population. These insights underscore the need for deeper biological characterization of this double‐refractory population and support the development of rational combination or sequential strategies in prospective, dedicated clinical trials (e.g., BsAbs with chemotherapy, targeted agents, or novel immunotherapies) to optimize patient management.

The Multivariate Shumilov analysis revealed elevated LDH levels at the initiation of the BsAb therapy, higher International Prognostic Index scores, and refractoriness to the last therapy as independent predictors of poor outcomes. The DESCAR‐T 3L CAR T‐cell study revealed high LDH levels, ECOG PS ≥ 2, very early progression, and elevated CRP and ferritin as adverse prognostic factors. In the current study, elevated CRP ≥ 30 mg/L, time between infusion and first progression, and ECOG ≥ 2 were identified as independent OS2 predictors. These reproducible and simple signals can aid in stratification and clinical trial prioritization for this poor‐prognosis double‐refractory population. We also explored the applicability of the established prognostic scores in our cohort. However, we could not validate the post‐CAR prognostic index (PCPI), which has shown promise in the 3L setting 57 because the DESCAR‐T registry does not systematically capture the number of extranodal sites at relapse, a key component of the score. Furthermore, although we assessed the HEMATOTOX score, this score did not demonstrate significant prognostic value for OS in our 2L population, likely because of the specific risk profile of patients failing early after receiving 2L CAR T‐cell therapy. 31 , 58 , 59 , 60

This study, which is based on a large multicenter real‐world cohort, provides a representative overview of current post‐CAR T‐cell management in France. The use of propensity score weighting strengthens the validity of comparative analyses, while the inclusion of both axi‐cel and liso‐cel recipients and the detailed characterization of relapse features increase the generalizability and clinical relevance of the findings.

Our study has several limitations inherent to its retrospective, registry‐based design. First, despite the use of propensity score matching, selection bias in treatment allocation remains possible as the specific rationale for physician choices (e.g., monotherapy vs. combinations) was not captured in the DESCAR‐T registry. Second, as this registry focuses primarily on the CAR T procedure itself, the lack of granular data—specifically pretreatment CD20 expression, exact number of BasAb administrations, or precise reasons for treatment discontinuation—limits our mechanistic understanding, although management followed national LYSA guidelines. 61 Third, the heterogeneity and small sample sizes of certain subgroups (notably HGBCL, n = 18, and specific combinations, n = 29) precluded dedicated multivariate or double‐hit lymphoma analyses. Additionally, the short median follow‐up (8.4 months) restricts long‐term response assessment, particularly for patients in complete remission. Finally, the enrichment of high‐risk patients (77% primary refractory) in the cohort may limit generalizability to more indolent disease profiles. Despite these limitations, this study provides crucial real‐world evidence on salvage strategies after 2L CAR T‐cell therapy failure and identifies key prognostic factors (CRP, ECOG PS, and time to progression) to guide clinical stratification.

The absence of improved outcomes compared with post‐3L CAR T‐cell failure supports the notion that relapse after CAR T‐cell therapy is a poor prognostic event at any treatment line, reflecting an intrinsically resistant and aggressive tumor biology. This underscores the urgent need for novel strategies rather than simply repositioning existing therapies. Combination approaches incorporating combination strategies, novel targeted agents, or agents that address the suppressive tumor microenvironment warrant investigation. Emerging data on anti‐CD22 CAR T‐cells (CAR22) with a 68% ORR and 14‐month median OS in patients with anti‐CD19 CAR‐refractory disease suggest that alternative antigen targeting may overcome some resistance mechanisms. 62 Prospective biomarker‐driven studies are needed to identify patients at the highest risk for early relapse who may benefit from consolidative strategies or maintenance approaches following 2L CAR T‐cell therapy. As CD20‐directed BsAbs are being increasingly incorporated into frontline therapy, the management of patients post‐CAR T‐cell failure represents a major and growing unmet medical need. Consequently, prospective clinical trials specifically designed for the post‐2L CAR T‐cell setting, rather than relying on extrapolation from heavily pretreated patients in the 3L setting and beyond, are critically needed.

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: Outcomes remain poor for patients with relapsed or refractory LBCL after 2L CAR T‐cell therapy, regardless of the salvage approach used. In patients who relapsed after 2L CAR T‐cell therapy, compared with other available strategies, BsAbs yielded slightly better outcomes, although OS remained very short. Early relapse within 6 months and elevated inflammatory markers may help to identify patients at the highest risk. These findings highlight the need for novel strategies and prospective studies to establish a SOC in this double‐refractory population.
